lesson_title: The Stadium That Fills in the Last Minute: Population Growth Explained
hook_text: Ten thousand years to seat the first billion people. Twelve years for the latest one.
clip_script: Imagine seating all of humanity in a giant stadium over 24 hours. For the first 23 hours and 45 minutes, people trickle in — a family here, a village there. By quarter to midnight there is just ONE billion inside. That is everything from the first farms to the year 1800. Then the last fifteen minutes happen — and SEVEN more billion pour through the gates. A new billion roughly every twelve years: 1974, 1987, 1999, 2011, eight billion by 2022. So what happened? Here is the twist: people did not start having more babies. Babies stopped DYING. For thousands of years high births were cancelled by famine, disease and dirty water. Then came food, clean water, vaccines, antibiotics — deaths collapsed, births carried on, and the gap between them blew the population upward. And the second twist almost nobody knows: the surge is already easing. The growth rate peaked in the late 1960s and has fallen ever since, because families everywhere are shrinking. South Africa went from six children per woman to about 2,3 — by choice, not force. The stadium is still filling. But the queue outside gets shorter every single year.
visual_style: A stadium timelapse with a 24-hour clock; near-empty stands for most of the day, then a flood of dots in the final minutes; a counter of billion-milestones; a closing shot of the queue thinning.
mood: Epic scale with a double twist.
pacing: Slow hush through the empty hours, explosive rush at quarter to midnight, calm surprising ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for doubling time, overpopulation and what actually slows growth.
